body.heading: The story everyone knows
paragraphs: The tale goes like this: around 1590, Galileo Galilei climbed the Leaning Tower of Pisa and dropped two balls of different weights before a crowd of professors. Both struck the ground together, demolishing Aristotle's claim that heavy objects fall faster, in a single dramatic moment.

It is a wonderful story. The trouble is the evidence: Galileo never described doing it. The account comes from his last student, Vincenzo Viviani, writing years after Galileo's death — and other scholars of the era did perform similar drops, with messier results than the legend admits.

body.heading: What Galileo actually did
paragraphs: Galileo's real method was subtler and more powerful. Falling objects move too fast to time with 17th-century clocks, so he slowed the fall: rolling bronze balls down a gently sloped, polished groove, timing them with a water clock and his own pulse.

From these patient experiments he found the rule: the distance a falling object travels grows with the square of the time. Double the time, quadruple the distance. That mathematical pattern — not a tower stunt — is what overturned the old physics and founded the science of motion.

body.heading: Why the legend survives
paragraphs: The tower story endures because it dramatises a real truth: Galileo insisted that nature, not authority, settles questions. He pointed his telescope at Jupiter in 1610 and saw moons circling another world — evidence anyone could check, and many did.
Science keeps the legend as a parable and the experiments as the proof. It is a good arrangement: let the story inspire you, then do what Galileo did, and measure.

takeaway: The tower drop is likely legend; Galileo's real breakthrough was rolling balls down ramps and finding the mathematics of falling.
